overview: This three-document file concerns a May 1946 request to permit Yomiuri Shimbun foreign correspondent Hiroshi Kitamura and his family to relocate from Stockholm, Sweden, to Zurich, Switzerland, so that he could continue his journalistic work. The United States Political Adviser for Japan forwarded the matter to the Department of State after receiving assurances that occupation intelligence authorities had no objection and that SCAP did not handle the return or movement of Japanese residents in Europe. Enclosures reproduce Kitamura’s radiogram to the Yomiuri office and an Imperial Japanese Government memorandum detailing the family members, Swiss visas, financial arrangements, and official request for permission.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 415 on Hiroshi Kitamura’s proposed travel to Zurich
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The Political Adviser requests State Department guidance on allowing Yomiuri correspondent Hiroshi Kitamura and his family to move from Stockholm to Zurich.
subfiles.summary: The despatch forwards a radiogram from Hiroshi Kitamura and a memorandum from the Imperial Japanese Government’s Central Liaison Office. It reports that the Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, has no objection to the proposed move and that SCAP does not consider itself responsible for the return or movement of Japanese residents in Europe. The Political Adviser therefore asks the Department of State for its comments.
keywords: United States Political Adviser for Japan

subfiles.title: Radiogram from Kitamura requesting transfer to Zurich
subfiles.to: Kori Tanaka and the Yomiuri Shimbun head office, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Kitamura asks the Yomiuri office to approve his transfer to Zurich so that he can continue working as a correspondent.
subfiles.summary: Kitamura states that a Swiss visa has already been granted and asks the newspaper’s headquarters to consent in principle to his transfer. He adds that Yoshimura is prepared to negotiate with Swiss financial authorities for the release of minimum living expenses from frozen Shokin funds under an Allied decision. The compressed cable language illustrates the practical financial and administrative obstacles facing a Japanese correspondent in postwar Europe.

subfiles.title: Central Liaison Office request for permission for the Kitamura family to enter Switzerland
subfiles.from: Central Liaison Office, Imperial Japanese Government
subfiles.to: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: The Japanese Government formally requests permission for Hiroshi Kitamura and his family to leave Sweden for Switzerland.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum explains that Yomiuri Shimbun has applied for permission for Kitamura, its Stockholm correspondent, to relocate with his family to Zurich. It identifies his wife Marie Louise and sons Hikaru and Tadashi and states that Swiss entry visas have already been issued to all four. It also reports that U.S. authorities in Sweden have no objection, subject to approval by General Headquarters, and notes that Kitamura intends to continue working as Yomiuri’s correspondent.

interest: The file offers a compact case study of how the movement of Japanese civilians and journalists in Europe was negotiated immediately after the Second World War. It is particularly useful for tracing the overlapping responsibilities—and uncertainty over jurisdiction—among the Japanese Government, SCAP, occupation intelligence, U.S. authorities in Europe, and the Department of State. The enclosures also preserve unusually specific biographical details about Kitamura’s family and reveal how visa status, frozen Japanese funds, and permission from newspaper headquarters shaped the revival of Japanese foreign news-gathering.
